textbookText: Isotopes are nuclei of the same element that have the same number of protons, but different numbers of neutrons.

For example, ordinary hydrogen (11𝐻), deuterium (12𝐻), and tritium (13𝐻) are all isotopes of the element hydrogen. Specific isotopes can be indicated by the element name, and the atomic mass number. For example, carbon-12 is another way of writing126𝐶.

The chemical properties of an atom are determined by its electron configuration. Because the numbers of electrons and protons are equal in a neutral atom, the chemical properties are essentially determined by Z. All the isotopes of a particular element have the same number of protons and electrons. So, these isotopes have almost identical chemical properties. However, the physical properties can differ dramatically. In particular, one isotope of an element may be highly radioactive, while another is quite stable. Bombarding materials with electrons, neutrons, or other particles can create radioactive isotopes.

Atoms and nuclei are much, much smaller than everyday objects. So, even though a kilogram may be a convenient unit for expressing the mass of apples or oranges, it is not particularly useful for measuring the mass of a proton or a carbon nucleus. For calculations involving nuclei and subatomic particles, it is often convenient to use a mass unit that is much smaller than the kilogram.

The atomic mass unit (u) is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of the carbon atom126𝐶. Now the number of molecules in 1 mole of carbon is6.02 × 1023 , Avogadro's constant, and since carbon is monoatomic, there are 6.02 × 1023 atoms of carbon. These have a mass of 12 g.

Thus, all nuclei have approximately the same density. This fact is of crucial importance in understanding nuclear structure. The nucleus of an atom is very small, massive, and hence extremely dense. All nuclei have a density of about 1017 kg m-3- about 1014 times denser than water.
